rewrites.4043CC13: By 2035 the goal must leave the province able to deliver its growth and share it. Visitor spend should reach the communities, measured against a reference point of 1% of foreign direct spend, R259 million a year at FY2025 levels (section 5.3). LTOs should hold stable funding, and tourism projects should reach financial close. The national tier should answer the province's asks, and the province should count its own tourism jobs and spend. Initiatives I12 to I18 carry the eight objectives, with objectives 16 and 17 sharing one forum in I15 (section 4.1).
rewrites.49C0A266: Two themes and eight objectives carry the goal. The first theme, investment, inclusion and sustainability, settles who benefits from growth, how it is paid for and how it lasts. It gives community product a local seller, keeps LTOs in service, holds growth within what each destination can carry and builds an investment pipeline that follows demand (objectives 13 to 15).
rewrites.191B68DE: Most LTOs are not operationally sustainable without municipal funding, and MFMA Circular No. 131 interrupted that funding, while the contracted-services route remains (Department of Economic Development)
rewrites.4719F49A: LTOs are kept in service by contract. Municipalities buy LTO services through lawful procurement, on a provincial practice note that sets out the route that remains under Circular 131, and the national ask narrows to the points still in dispute. The arrangement also tests the Blueprint's district model (objective 16). From 2029 the service agreements carry a development mandate and enter IDPs with reporting, through the Provincial Treasury's district reviews.
rewrites.17C8AE4A: Growth to 2035 has to stay within what the destination can carry. Water scarcity acts as a hard ceiling on visitor load in high-growth nodes such as the Garden Route, and the flagship nature sites run near capacity in season (section 2.4). The pressure weighs most where tourism weighs most. In 2023 tourist spend equalled 15.6% of GDPR in the Overberg and 16.8% on the West Coast, against 6.7% in the Metro. The Garden Route and Central Karoo reviews give identical series, which the Treasury is to confirm (section 5.4).[^357]
rewrites.58E44938: The evidence is dated and site-specific, but it does not add up to a provincial picture. No source puts a provincial figure on tourism revenue at risk from weather or water. The capacity figures for George and Knysna are conditional and do not certify spare capacity for a hotel (section 2.5).
rewrites.75BF16F2: The work runs in three strands. The first is adaptation and continuity. In 2027 and 2028 DEDAT and Wesgro's Research unit build a climate and weather risk register for sites and routes, starting with the dated losses (section 4.3). Wesgro routes itineraries around Meiringspoort while it is closed. The second is ordinary resource and ecological capacity. Readiness is assessed by node or supply zone, and continuity arrangements are tested, before public money promotes more demand there. The quality charter carries sustainability checks on the Mossel Bay model (objective 11). The third is emissions mitigation: Wesgro reports absolute resource use and emissions beside per-night intensity.
rewrites.4695779A: The growth case needs capital where the current pipeline does not reach. Visitors who travel beyond the Metro need beds, a booking route and finished product. The communities need assets a local seller can run. Yet committed capital goes to the air gaps and leaves the regional ones open (section 2.4). The province does not lack capital works. It lacks capital aimed at tourism outside the Metro.
rewrites.6F1A2A48: Tourism funding is also tight, and below peer destinations (section 2.5). Fiscal pressure is prompting consideration of a tourism levy. The Department of Mobility sees a need for climate, development, blended-finance and private-sector models to fund tourism-enabling mobility. Its draft land transport framework goes further and plans its own business case for a tourist levy, to fund tourism transport. Much of the product gap will fall to private capital, which moves only where a case is ready.[^365]
rewrites.59D4F61B: The accommodation gap shows what is at stake, and it is a product question rather than a missing tier. George already has a branded, conference-capable hotel, the Protea Hotel by Marriott George King George, with 109 rooms and four event rooms. What is missing differs by place (section 2.4). The Garden Route is short of quality-graded hotels for midweek, conference and business travel. Mossel Bay reports that limited upper-upscale hotel capacity, particularly a recognised brand able to host conferences, holds back its higher-value and business demand.[^366]
rewrites.6572EF60: Source: Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026 (IR; the ~R11.3bn Cape Town International headline itemises to R9.94bn on p103); Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026 (SIR); SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026 (SCIP). No deliverable gives a Western Cape tourism funding-gap figure.
rewrites.0556127E: The evidence shows a gap in direction as much as in volume. The district tables list a large capital pipeline, and their gap columns show that none of it reaches regional product, SME bookability or township product. That finding is an inference from the tables rather than a statement the source makes, and no source gives a Western Cape tourism funding-gap figure. Kliptown is the warning case: capital built before an operator earned no operating income (section 2.2).
rewrites.6EF02F17: Routes to capital and approval exist, though none is a tourism pipeline. The Tourism Transformation Fund has approved 43 transactions worth more than R510.51 million nationally, which are approvals and not disbursements. The IDC takes tourism business cases, and DEDAT runs a Red Tape Reduction service and helpline. A scored pipeline gives each of these routes cases to work on.
rewrites.2EFF19AE: Wesgro should build the tourism investment pipeline the gap tables imply, and commit public capital only where demand has been shown. In 2027 and 2028 Wesgro's investment promotion team scores the gaps for return, jobs and inclusion and prepares the first investment cases (section 4.3). Each accommodation case starts from the destination-and-product test run with I10: which configuration, price point, location or capacity is missing, and where. The test compares refurbishment and better use of existing stock with new build on lifecycle cost. The first cases cover the conference-capable and mid-market product the test confirms in secondary nodes, and accommodation at De Hoop and on Route 62.
rewrites.2EC77CCC: The levy case is set against its legal route and timing. A municipal tax and a provincial tax each follow a statutory process that can take more than a year. The case therefore assumes no levy proceeds for essential near-term operations, which stay on existing budgets. The case also weighs a new charge against the voluntary 1% the industry already collects through TOMSA.
rewrites.7733E5B5: The evidence agrees on the problem and is thin on the fix. What is needed is a shared growth agenda with clear decision rights and joint delivery plans. No source maps decision rights by tier beyond one summary table. The national tier is barely heard: the Department of Tourism and Stats SA spoke only to data, and SA Tourism has no recorded view. The first task is to hear the national tier directly and write down who decides what. For the districts, one design is already on record. The Tourism Blueprint 2030 recommends tourism coordination at district level, with regional tourism organisations run as non-profits, funded by district municipalities and seating the LTOs. It also asks for the LTO model to be set in law. The Blueprint's targets were set before COVID-19, so this action plan treats its model as a position to test, not a settled design. The mandate settlement below and the LTO service agreements in objective 13 test it against Circular 131.[^372]
rewrites.45BB84FB: Fifteen of the sixteen organisations heard raised collaboration, and the channels already exist in the industry associations' joint forum (JAMMS), the bid teams and the tour-operator forums. The task is to turn existing forums into one joint plan.
rewrites.0C1C77D3: Wesgro uses the forums that exist and gives them a development agenda and one joint plan. In 2027 it adopts JAMMS as the single channel to the associations, because FEDHASA expects consultation through it to cascade more efficiently than approaching each body separately. It adds the Tour Guides Association, so frontline operators have a voice. It designs sector councils for wine, business events, adventure and culture inside Steerco's structure (section 4.7), and they run from 2029 (section 4.3).[^381]
rewrites.175C1247: Every target to 2035 depends on fixing this. The plan tracks spend, season and spread beside arrivals. No source yet gives visitor spend by district (section 5.3). The nearest measure is tourist spend as a share of each district's GDPR. The Provincial Treasury's district reviews report it, from Wesgro and S&P Global Market Intelligence data. Even arrivals are counted in ways that are not reconciled. Appendix A2 sets out three measures: ACSA passenger arrivals, SA Tourism tourist arrivals and the growth model's international arrivals. OAG's air series adds a fourth count. Without a shared data layer, no intervention can be targeted or measured.[^386]
rewrites.2D3C5CF9: Wesgro's Research unit agrees data-sharing terms with each data holder and runs one indicator register and dashboard, as section 5.5 sets out. In 2027 it builds the register and agrees terms with ACSA, SA Tourism, Stats SA, Cape Town Tourism, the site operators and the booking platforms. It also agrees terms with the Provincial Treasury for the data behind the Treasury's reviews and with the Department of Mobility for its Integrated Transport Hub.
rewrites.6CDD3896: New Zealand shows what shared data can support. Data shared between tourism bodies and airlines is one of four enablers of its route-accountable marketing, with airport readiness, route incentives and co-investment tied to route KPIs. That marketing reports a return of about NZ$55 million in 2023/24 (section 2.2). Valencia is the realism check: integrating data systems across institutions there can create technical and organisational challenges. The condition is consent. Each data holder must sign, so the number of agreements signed is the first measure of progress (section 4.3).[^392]
rewrites.159A92DF: Visas, air rights, airport capacity and policing shape how many visitors reach the province and how safe they feel. The province holds few of these levers. National government holds visa rules, border compliance and air service agreements. The province holds safety programmes and local government holds basic services. ACSA, a national body, holds the runway (section 2.5). Escalation is the province's main tool for the national share.[^393]
rewrites.2E2D65D4: African entry rules differ passport by passport. Ghana and Kenya ordinary passports carry 90 days a year, and Botswana and Zimbabwe sit in the 90-day category. Nigeria is not ordinarily exempt, and no waiver covers SADC as a whole (section 2.5). The reported ETA list covers 17 African markets, Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria among them, yet access to the platform does not change a traveller's visa status. No comparable processing-time series exists for the visa-required African markets. Regional event demand therefore cannot yet be set against entry performance.
rewrites.35FA4DC3: The province's own safety services already run. DEDAT's 2026/27 Annual Performance Plan funds the City's Tourist and Visitor Safety Unit at high-volume central-city attractions. It also runs a Tourism Safety and Support service and convenes a Provincial Tourism Safety Forum twice a year. Cape Town Tourism's TravelWise network and the City's 24/7 visitor-support service run beside them (section 2.5). The City records 2,895 motorist assists by N2 patrols from September 2024 to January 2026. An assist is not a crime rate, and the open questions are coverage, eligibility and handoffs between services, not existence.
rewrites.5A3A6C5F: The initiative runs two workstreams, and the first is access escalation. Wesgro runs a standing escalation agenda at Steerco. Each item names the decision, the national body that holds it and the date the province asks for. Wesgro tables the first agenda in 2027 (section 4.3). The agenda covers entry for China, India, the Middle East and Africa, air service agreements and immigration throughput at Cape Town International.
rewrites.1E60CDCB: A vacancy does not prove a skills shortage. Industry employment totals cannot identify unfilled posts. A post can also stay open because of pay, seasonal contracts or the cost of commuting, none of which training fixes. The analysis has to separate skills scarcity from the conditions of the job.
rewrites.620B2322: Wesgro and DEDAT commission a tourism labour analysis in 2027, and it is employer-linked. It draws on employers' own records by occupation, place and season. It fixes a provincial employment baseline and definition, tests the 300,000 ambition and identifies the occupations and skills the growth case needs. It separates skills scarcity from pay, seasonal contracts and commuting, because each needs a different response. The test starts with whether the ambition counts direct or total jobs. It starts from the department's 2023 figures and asks DEDAT for the method and definition behind them. The analysis feeds the economic measures workstream (I16), which sets the jobs baseline in 2027. Chapter 5 sets the targets at Gate 1, at the end of 2028 (sections 4.7 and 5.3).
rewrites.10E9D5BF: The three goals make one case. Conversion turns interest into visits, seats pace it at the peak and supply work pays only where visitors can find and reach the product. Each needs the enabling base to last.
rewrites.75B9AD44: The growth model sets out three cases from the 2025 base of 1,498,829 arrivals: 1,822,634 in 2035 on the conservative case, 2,175,778 on the base case and 2,516,282 on the accelerated case. The cases differ by intervention, not by demand potential. Each step of the growth case therefore rests on a named set of interventions. The first two steps draw on Goals 1 and 2 alone. Goal 3 adds arrivals only on the third step, through the three-tier agenda and national escalation (objectives 16 and 19). Its other six objectives decide whether growth is shared, funded, sustained and measured.[^411]
rewrites.791B8829: **Seats pace growth at the peak.** Airlines have extended capacity past the growth model's 1.8 million seat marker, and the 2.5 million target needs about 3.1 million inbound seats (section 2.4). Relief at Cape Town International arrives about 2032 for the international terminal and about 2033 for the runway (section 2.4). Until then, peak growth comes from larger aircraft and added frequency on the full routes and from hub-carrier capacity (objectives 5, 6 and 7). Domestic connections can also grow through George, whose terminal doubles by 2028 or 2029.[^414]

inserts.text: The second theme, governance and leadership, settles who decides and who measures. It aligns the three tiers of government, turns industry forums into one joint plan and agrees how data is shared (objectives 16 to 18). The same theme holds two further objectives. Objective 19 takes the national deficits in infrastructure, visas and safety to the tier that holds them. Objective 20 commissions the labour analysis a skills plan will rest on.

From 2029 climate risk enters municipal IDPs, with reporting. The route exists: the Provincial Treasury writes its district reviews to inform IDPs and budgets, and they already carry environmental risk data.[^361]

From 2029 Wesgro takes the cases to investors. DEDAT, the Department of Mobility and the City of Cape Town then test blended-finance vehicles and one levy case for the visitor economy. The pipeline is refreshed each year.

In 2028 the dashboard goes live with automated arrivals, seat and cruise feeds and quarterly digital tracking (section 4.3). The dashboard sets campaign results against airline capacity and hotel trends, and annual or twice-yearly brand research sits beside it. Wesgro also starts to measure meetings, incentives and exhibitions. Meetings are absent from consolidated provincial statistics, and the scale of the other two is unverified.[^390]

The visa asks start from DEDAT's visa regime study, which ranks published processing times first and visa exemption for China, India and Nigeria second. The agenda takes the reforms that bear on visitors and first checks what has moved since 2024. Wesgro's Advocacy and Advisory unit was set up to build evidence-based policy feedback on levers the province does not control. Once Wesgro confirms its remit, the unit runs the agenda day to day. Research and Destination Marketing build the evidence for each ask, market by market. Stakeholder insights already point to the evidence needed: the safety issues most damaging to demand and the access barriers across air, visas and onward travel.[^398]

queries.issue: Q5: no actor named. Prescriptive or passive sentences in "The course of action" whose actor is not given by the previous sentence, and where the "Who acts" row is "With partners" with several stakeholders or has no matching row. Left unchanged. paraIds: 116676CF ("Safety plans follow"; "thresholds agreed before launch"); 3FD9C372 ("Three conditions are added"; extortion controls "are in place"); 75BF16F2 ("Readiness is assessed ... continuity arrangements are tested": row lists DEDAT; municipalities; site operators) and the new paragraph split from it ("climate risk enters municipal IDPs": no row in the table); 2EFF19AE split paragraph ("The pipeline is refreshed each year"); 2EC77CCC ("The levy case is set against its legal route"); 38632FA1 ("Route work runs alongside": row gives Wesgro, Air Access); 3B2D83C3 ("the joint industry plan is agreed and reviewed each year"); 0E5C71C0 ("Handoffs between services are tested"; "The workstream is reviewed at the end of 2028"); 3A69BBEA ("Safety compacts follow"; "responses to the national asks are logged and followed up").
queries.options: (a) Leave the passives, since the plan assigns no accountability. (b) Author names the acting body for each. (c) Use "Wesgro and its partners" throughout for "With partners" rows.

queries.issue: Q5: "the province" acts as a body ("the province leads by escalation", "the province asks Home Affairs", "the province must move decisions", "the province should count its own tourism jobs"). The text does not say whether the actor is Wesgro, Steerco, DEDAT or the Western Cape Government, so nothing was changed. paraIds: 536A88B8, 4043CC13, 24F5FC0B, 3B2D83C3, 7FC79505, 159A92DF, 194CE623, 5298561A, 26941C03, 390DB324, 604FC4B0.

queries.issue: The opening sentence has Wesgro "commit public capital only where demand has been shown", but the "Who acts" table gives public and community assets to municipalities (row 6) and Wesgro only builds the pipeline. It is unclear whose capital is meant.
queries.options: (a) Leave. (b) Recast as a rule for the pipeline, for example that public capital follows shown demand, without making Wesgro the one that commits it.

queries.issue: The runway repeat was reduced to "about 2033 (section 2.4)", so the paragraph no longer mentions the ACSA December 2029 schedule. Footnote 414 still cites the ACSA presentation (Travel News, Aug 2026) for it.

queries.issue: R3: "carriers are expected to raise fares before they add seats" names no one who expects it. Footnote 415 points to the Aviation Market Assessment, but the paragraph does not say so. Left unchanged.
